newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico shares rocket to 8th straight record close.
newsitem.headline: Mexico shares rocket to 8th straight record close.

text.p: Mexican stocks soared to their eighth record close in a row on Friday as more good economic news kept the bulls charging amid a market awash with foreign capital.
"The market has broken pre-set objectives," said Hector Jimenez, an analyst at the Inverlat brokerage.
The blue chip IPC share index gained 85.47 points, or 1.96 percent, to a record of 4,439.14.
Trading was very heavy at 181.2 million shares and clearly reflected a heavy inflow of foreign investors.
"An additional kicker came in terms of the retail sales figures, which were a pleasant surprise," said Felix Boni, research chief at ING-Barings in Mexico.
Mexico's National Statistics Institute reported that retail sales during April had increased by 6.6 percent over the same month last year.
The latest Reuters survey of 13 financial firms had forecast an average increase of just 0.17 percent.
Analysts said Mexico was considered attractive within Latin America as, despite recent gains, it was still relatively cheap in valuation terms and still lagged behind Brazil.

"It (Mexico) is a bull market, as is Latin America. Investors, particularly in North America, are just pouring money into the region," said Geoffrey Dennis, investment strategist at HSBC-James Capel in New York.
The IPC has gained 11.85 percent so far in June, and far outstripped analysts' projections.
Nonetheless, the IPC is far behind Brazil's Bovespa in year-to-date terms, having gained 32.08 percent vs. 72.17 percent by its counterpart in Sao Paulo, Brazil.

Retailer Cifra's A or preferred shares were the most heavily traded, and gained 38 centavos (5 cents) to 14.18 pesos ($1.78). Fellow retailer Controladora Comercial Mexicana also posted strong gains at brisk trade, and ended up 14 centavos (2 cents) to 7.08 pesos (89 cents).

Telmex climbed 50 centavos (6 cents) to a record close in pesos of 19.30 ($2.42), while the telecommunication's firm's ADRs ended up 1-1/4 on Wall Street at 48-1/2, their highest level since a shock devaluation sent Mexican markets slumping in December 1994. Telmex had traded at more than 70 on Wall Street during February 1994.
